description.value: Grubber's Market, a stolen apple, and a girl the whole city is about to start looking for.

Suddenly the stallkeeper jabs his finger at you and screams, *'Stop, thief!'*

One of the mercenaries happens to be wandering by at that moment. He hears the stallkeeper's shouts and comes running straight for you!

Then there is a loud screech, and something gray and hairy scampers out from under the mercenary's feet. He stumbles, trips, and pitches headlong into the fruit stall. Fruit scatters everywhere. The stallkeeper is wailing and berating the mercenary, who is covered with juice and slimy pulp.

The saddle is way too huge for you to nick. Anyway, horses make you nervous.
You need a belt in order to wear this thing.

The crowd is thick with shoppers and merchants alike, all shouting at each other, shuffling and squeezing against each other to get a better look at the merchandise. Some of them try to give the mercenaries a slightly wider berth, but elsewhere it's shoulder to shoulder. Staying out of sight should be easy, as long as you keep moving.
Some of the marketfolk glance at you; a few put their hands protectively around their moneypurses. But no one seems interested in having a conversation with a common street urchin.
It's no use; these people just want to get on with their business and be left alone.
'Here, you! Scamper off, why don't you?'
The shopper roughly shoulders you aside.
The shopper waves you off, irritated.
'Take it somewhere else, kid, before I call the guard.'
This many bodies, pressed this close together on a morning this hot, is not exactly the most pleasant thing your nose has encountered.
With dozens of people around you constantly chattering, muttering, arguing and haggling, it is difficult to make out anything specific.
The walls are too high, and you cannot get a handhold.
The stalls are spread throughout the market below.
This is a relatively clear part of the market; most of the stalls are deeper in.
This part of the market is reserved for Teisha's tent. Most of the stalls are elsewhere.
There aren't any stalls here inside Teisha's tent.
You can't really see much of the stalls from back here behind them.
There aren't any stalls back here in the alley.
The stallkeeper shoos you away. 'Customers on the outside!' he shouts.
The stalls are too heavy to tip over.
The awnings are high out of your reach.
Looking straight up, you can see four support wires attached to the top of the center post, stretching in four directions.
The wires are too high up for you to reach, and you can't get to where they are attached on the ground.
You can't see the market from back here in the alley.
You can see the northwest corner of the market from up here.

The market spreads out beneath you in all directions.
The market smells of a mixture of all sorts of odors: dust and sweat, leather and sawdust, spices, fruits, and groceries.
The market is a cacophony of sounds, with dozens of merchants hawking their wares and scores of shoppers haggling over the price.

It smells delicious here.

It is relatively quiet and peaceful up here, although the sounds of the market drift up faintly from below.
You smell nothing unexpected.
You keep your ears pricked.
You need to find a way behind the stalls to get to the post.

You can't climb up the smooth, tight canvas.
The wall of the storehouse is too high and too smooth to climb.

You're totally hidden back here, so there's no one to stop you from climbing. By the time you're high enough for people to see you, you're also high enough that no one will notice anyway; no one ever bothers to look up in Grubber's Market. After a minute or so of grunting and sweating, you reach the top.
After a minute or so of grunting and sweating, you reach the top.
With speed borne of panic, you scamper up the wooden post.
It's all too far away for you to do more than look at it.
Nothing is on sale.
You'd sooner go hungry than steal from Teisha. She's your friend.
You'd love to, but you haven't any money.
You realize suddenly that this is exactly what you need: the perfect disguise!
The perfect disguise, if only you could afford one.
'What do you want?' snaps the stallkeeper.

'So, what are you selling today?' you ask, trying to sound casual.

The merchant sneers at you. 'You have any coin?'

'You know anything about these mercenaries running around Grubber's?' you ask.

'Only that they're bad for business,' mutters the stallkeeper. 'I don't know who hired them, but the Lord's Guard ought to run them off.'

'I'd like one of those, please,' you say, pointing.

The merchant sneers at you. 'You have any coin?'

'Yes,' you respond indignantly, 'and lots of it.'

The stallkeeper snorts derisively. 'If you've half a penny that isn't stolen from somewhere, I'll sell my stall to the monkey. Now go bother someone else before I call those mercenaries over here myself!'

'Um, no,' you say.

The stallkeeper rolls his eyes. 'Do I look like I have time to gab at you all day? Beat it, kid.'

'Uh, never mind.'

'Whatever,' the stallkeeper mutters, and goes back to nervously scanning the crowd.
'Yeah, fine, scram,' the stallkeeper mutters.
The stallkeeper suddenly looks exasperated. 'Didn't I tell you to take it somewhere else?'
'I said, beat it!' the stallkeeper yells.
'I said, scram!' the stallkeeper yells.
'I said, get out of here!' the stallkeeper yells.

Suddenly you hear someone shouting just outside: 'Hey, any of you dims check inside this tent yet?'

Teisha's face turns white. 'Hurry, Jack!' she hisses, 'Out the back way!'

Teisha's face falls as you stumble back into the tent. 'You're still here?' she asks. 'I'd hoped you'd gotten away by now.'

'Now that you mention it, I am a bit spooked,' you say, trying to catch your breath. 'There's a bunch of big guys with swords out there, chasing me all over the market!'

Teisha frowns. 'Big guys with — you mean mercenaries? In Grubber's?' She peeks out through the front flap. 'Brigid help us,' she mutters, glancing back at you. 'Don't tell me what they're after you for — I don't want to know.'

'No, really,' you say, in a not-quite-steady voice. 'Everything's just tricky.'

Teisha smirks. 'Uh-huh. You know I don't just sit by myself in this silk tent all day, don't you, Jack? I do have some idea of what's going on in the world outside, you know. I know there are mercenaries searching Grubber's, and I'm guessing they're probably after you.' Her voice softens, and she puts her hand on your shoulder. 'Don't worry, Jack. I don't need to know what you did to get them after you. I won't turn you in.'

'I need help, Teisha,' you tell her plaintively. 'I need somewhere to hide.'

Teisha sighs. Although you know she cares about you, you also know that Teisha is a smart, practical woman, and first and foremost she is worried about losing her customers. 'All right,' she says, 'you can stay in here as long as you like, but if the mercenaries decide to search the place I can't stop them. Probably your best bet is to slip out that way—' she points to the narrow gap in the back wall of the tent. 'I'll pretend I never saw you.'

Teisha smiles at you warmly.
Teisha brushes a loose thread from the sleeve of one of her gowns.
Teisha toys with her measuring cord, spinning it idly.

'I know that different merchants set up their stalls on different days of the week,' you say. 'So who's selling what today?'

'Well, there's the fruit stall on the northeast corner, but that's there every day,' says Teisha. 'To the north is a grocer's stall; a hat seller to the southeast; to the west is an herb seller and the gem merchant; and the leatherworker and weaponsmith have set up shop on the south end. The inner ring is me, a rope merchant, a pottery merchant, and that awful candlemaker — the stench has been driving off my customers all morning.'

'As I said,' says Teisha, 'there's the fruit stall to the northeast; the grocer to the north; the hat seller to the southeast; the herb seller and the gem merchant to the west; the leatherworker and weaponsmith to the south; and me, the rope merchant, the potter merchant, and the candlemaker in the inner ring.'

'What's that behind your tent?' you ask, nodding towards the back exit.

'There's nothing back there except the central pole holding up the big awning over the market,' Teisha says. 'That's why all the merchants want this spot,' she adds, '...it's got the best shade.'
'I told you already,' says Teisha, 'it's just a big pole.'

'These clothes are all so beautiful,' you say. 'Do you make them yourself?'

Teisha smiles. 'Some of them,' she says. 'Most of them I sell on consignment. One of these days, I'm going to clear enough profit to rent a shop on Commerce Street and move out of this hot, smelly tent.'
'Like I said,' says Teisha, 'some of them I make myself, some I sell for others.'

'The gem merchant sounds like he's got a real vendetta against that monkey,' you remark. 'What's the story with them?'

Teisha rolls her eyes. 'That pesky thing came in on the fruit vendor's wagon yesterday and just made itself at home. Now it's all over the place, bothering everybody. Fortunately, it likes shiny things more than it likes women's clothes. Oh, and bananas. The little rodent loves bananas. Constantly drops the peels on the roof of my tent.'
'I already told you,' says Teisha, 'it just runs around, eats bananas, and steals anything shiny that isn't nailed down.'

'It seems like everyone has an opinion about Baron Fossville, lately,' you remark. 'What's yours?'

Teisha laughs. 'So you've noticed it too, huh? I don't usually like to talk politics, which means I haven't had much in the way of conversation in Grubber's Market lately.' She shrugs. 'I don't like his high taxes, but who does? Fossville doesn't strike me as a very nice person, but I guess he doesn't have to be.'
'I told you,' says Teisha, 'I don't like him very much, but there's not much use complaining.'

I don't see why it's so interesting, frankly. What they do miles away in the capital doesn't have much to do with how many cloaks I sell today.')
(TODO during play-testing — 'See anything you like?' asks Teisha, with a teasing smile. She knows perfectly well you couldn't afford so much as a ribbon. 'Don't be a stranger, Jack.')

You strain to hear what the men are saying, but can't make out the words. Maybe if you got some elevation, you could hear better.
The men are still talking outside the alley.
The voices just outside the alley continue their conversation.
You can still hear the men at the entrance to the alley talking.
You can still hear the voices talking just outside the alley.
Those men are still talking right outside the alley. Something — an intuition? — tells you it would be a good idea to stay out of sight for the moment.
Those men are still talking right outside the alley. Better stay out of sight until they leave.
So what are they doing here, you wonder? And come to think of it, where are the Lord's Guards, anyway?
You listen carefully to what the mercenaries are saying...
'...we know he skulks Grubber's most mornings, so spread out quick, cover all streets from the square,' growls one of them, evidently the group's leader.

The leader spits on the dusty ground. 'Keep your eyes open and don't take guff. But for the love of Brigid, keep your tempers and your swords sheathed unless you really need 'em. Ain't bein' paid to toss the locals.'

'And keep sharp!' the leader snaps. 'Remember this is a kid we're lookin' for. Kids move fast, stay out of sight, slip through crowds easy. I find out later he got away under your nose, I'll have it off!'

Suddenly, that bit of apple you swallowed a minute ago turns into a cold, hard chunk in your belly.

'Now, everyone memorize the description.' The leader pulls a dirty, folded bit of parchment from his belt and squints at it. 'Shoulder-length brown hair,' he reads, haltingly. 'Green eyes. Slight of build. Ten, maybe twelve spans high.' He holds his hand out flat, at what happens to be exactly your height. 'Usually wears a hat and a gray cloak.'

He refolds the parchment and jams it back into his belt. 'You dims got all that?'

The others nod.

'Okay, go!' barks the leader, and the mercenaries set out in several directions, moving at a brisk walk. Two men go to the north gates and start shoving them closed; the others enter the crowded market and start shoving their way through the suddenly flabbergasted crowds.

Your heart sinks. This is *definitely* not good.
You nimbly hop up on top of the crates; from there, it's only a short scramble to the roof of the market.

As you climb back down the crates, one of them wobbles and your foot slips. You tumble loudly to the cobblestones. 'Stupid! Clumsy!' you mutter, scrambling to your feet.

From the street, you hear, 'What was that? Check the alley!'

Two mercenaries rush in and spot you immediately. They approach warily, their arms spread wide.

You're in trouble now...
You try to scramble up the crates, but one of the mercenaries grabs your ankle and drags you back down!

The rooftop is steep and slick, and the tiles have been known to come loose and fall off. It's precarious enough just staying here in one spot. If you're to make your escape, you'll have to make it down on the ground.
You can't quite make out what they're saying from up here.
The mercenaries have stopped talking. All you can hear now is the constant chock! of the axe.
You can't do anything to the mercenaries while you're way up here.
The axe's steady chocking noise is very loud, even from up here.
You can't do anything to the axe while you're way up here.
You hear shouting coming from all quarters of the market. If the mercenaries saw where you landed, they'll be after you in no time.

Mercenaries burst through the crowd from three different directions. They grab you and slam you to the ground, knocking the breath from your lungs.

'Gotcha, you little runt!' someone growls in your ear.
There's no time for that! You've got to run!
You sprint through the crowd.
You dive through the crowd.
You weave through the crowd.
You dodge through the crowd.
You race through the crowd.
You dash for Teisha's tent, but it's no good — the mercenaries have planted themselves outside it and are scanning the crowd. You backpedal quickly before they can spot you.
Not that way — the alley is a dead end!
No good — the mercenaries have closed the north gates and aren't letting anyone through. Your only chance is east, further into the city!

'Jack, what are you doing?!' Teisha cries, 'Get out of—oof!'

The mercenaries charge in, knocking Teisha and racks of silk garments to the floor. A rock-hard fist closes around your upper arm. 'Gotcha!' the mercenary yells. The other one starts hollering for his companions as they drag you out of the tent.

The captain soon arrives, followed by two more of his men. They take your other arm as their leader smiles. 'Good work, dims. Got ourselves a nice little commission with this one.' And before you can react, he takes a sack of black cloth from his belt and jerks it down over your head.

Everything goes dark. You can't breathe. You struggle, but you can no more break the iron grip on your arms than you could uproot a tree. The men holding you curse. Dimly, you hear shouts from the crowd — someone protesting this rough treatment of a child.

'Don't worry, m'lady,' laughs the mercenary leader. 'We'll treat the little rat nice an' gentle. Like this, see?'

Something huge and heavy crashes into your head, and the rest of your senses are ripped away. Why they wanted you, you never awake to find out.
You can hear Teisha yelling shrilly at the mercenaries behind you — then her tirade is cut off abruptly amidst grunted curses. Someone is fumbling with the back flap of the tent!

The mercenaries burst out of the tent. With nowhere to run, you are quickly overwhelmed. They drag you back out to the market (dimly you see Teisha sitting amidst her scattered silks, nursing a bloody nose) and hold you firmly while calling to their comrades.

One of the mercenaries tries to climb after you, but can't get more than a few feet up before sliding back. Looks like you're safe for the time being — but they're already heatedly discussing how to get you down, and there are only so many ways you can go from here.
Another of the mercenaries tries his luck climbing the post, but his callused fingers can't get a grip on the wood.
One of the mercenaries kicks the post in frustration.
The mercenaries continue to shout and point.
More mercenaries are squeezing into the tiny square behind Teisha's tent.
The sounds of heated debate drift up from below. You just make out the word, 'fire'.

One of the mercenaries runs back out through Teisha's tent.

You just have time to notice the grins on the mercenaries' faces, and the fact that none of them are trying to catch you, before the ground fills your sight and everything goes black.

You pull and struggle, but the man is just too strong.
You beat on the mercenary's arms with your fists, but the man is just too strong.
You claw the mercenary's arms skin with your fingernails, but the man is just too strong.

You dash away into the crowd, weaving between customers and pushing your way through the thickest knots of people. The mercenaries pound after you, yelling and shoving people out of their way, but they're too big and too slow, and you quickly manage to lose them.

Thinking quickly, you kick the mercenary in the shin.

The heat and fumes from the candlemaker's tallow pots make this stall an unpleasant place to loiter. The east end of Commerce Street winds through an upper-class residential neighborhood before ending up at Lord's Market. Behind spiked, iron fences stand the 'city cottages' of Toresal's wealthy merchants and nobility, built tall and narrow to make the best use of limited real estate.

Three stately houses are built close together on the north side of the road: Black Gate Estate to the northwest; Red Gate Estate to the north; and the Jacobs family mansion to the northeast. The street itself continues east and west, and the City Park lies to the south. {pieter-bodyguard}

Black Gate Estate is the home of Baron Fossville, the current Lord of Toresal since the old Duke's death (though he has yet to be fully confirmed). It is a somber building of dark flagstone and slate, although you've heard the Baron keeps a beautiful rooftop garden.

This is where the Duke and former Lord of Toresal lived, until his death several years ago. Now it stands empty, slowly crumbling. No one has ever made an attempt to claim the property, and the Baron seems content to let it remain vacant.
The front gates are securely locked.
The front gates are closed.
The front gates are open.

Jacobs the Elder is rumored to be the richest merchant in Toresal. His lavish city residence is built to resemble a miniature castle, complete with turrets, crenellations, and a heavy portcullis over the front door.
All the castle-style architecture on Jacobs' mansion is a bit ostentatious.

The park is a couple of acres of open meadow and sparse woods in the middle of the city, set aside by the previous Lord to promote health and relaxation among Toresal's citizens. It still sees strollers and the occasional picnicker by day, although it's become infamous as a haunt for cutpurses by night. The park is surrounded by a high stone wall, with a gate on the north side.
The fence is too high to climb, and topped with sharp iron spikes to boot.

Germaise the Baker is a tall, thin man from the south. He has a thick accent and likes to stroke his sparse moustaches with his fingertips while he talks — the lower half of his face is almost always covered with a grayish coating of flour. He's a shameless flirt, always eyeballing the young ladies who come into his store. It's moments like those that make you grateful for your disguise.
Germaise's moustache looks like a caterpillar with particularly dirty feet walked across his upper lip and left tracks, but he sure is proud of it.
The mound of dough is twice the size of Germaise's head, and he keeps punching it and squeezing it for all he's worth. It looks like a great way to work out your frustration.

Holstenoffer is a squat brick of a man, with a scarred bulldog's face and sailors' tattoos covering his arms from the wrists all the way up to his rolled-up sleeves. He's friendly enough and loves to gossip, but he has a tendency to gesticulate with his cleaver in hand, which sometimes makes conversation with him a tense and athletic affair.

Holstenoffer calls his cleaver 'Big Molly,' and often talks to it as though it were a pet. The side of the blade is tarnished and dull from years of use, but the edge is sharp enough to hack through thick muscle and bone like they were pudding.
Holstenoffer's tattoos are a solid blue tangle of swirling designs, covering his arms from his wrists all the way up to his rolled-up sleeves.
Olgan Minor is short but muscular, with a lined face and graying, military-cut hair. He says nothing as you browse his wares, but his eyes seem to bore right into you.
{lords-market-by-day}{lords-market-by-night} {gallows-erected}{gallows-erected-seen} {fossville-on-the-platform} {pieter-bodyguard}

A large window, trimmed in fine, dark wood, lets light into the front of the shop. A clothier's dummy dressed in a smartly cut tunic stands in front of a velvet backdrop, advertising the latest fashion to be found inside.

The sign above this store is painted with a necklace of pearls. The windows are blocked with thick (but decorative) iron bars, and the door sports a heavy lock. An engraved brass plaque reads 'Sandler and Son.'
A discreet placard next to the door reads 'Chorus Brothers.' The remainder of the windowless storefront is painted blue.
A fine clothier's, a jewelry store, and a moneylender's shop lie northeast, east, and southeast, respectively.

Most of the people wandering about Lord's Market are well dressed servants of the upper class (even for merchandise as nice as this, rich people rarely do their own shopping). Everyone looks to be in a dreadful hurry, with dreadfully important business to attend to, and no one affords you so much as a second glance.
The lampposts are unlit during the day.

The walls are hung with tasteful curtains, and a deep, soft carpet covers the floor. Several clothier's dummies stand about the room, displaying gorgeous formal court apparel for both men and women. The street lies west. {clothier-distaste}{clothier-waiting-to-serve} {pieter-bodyguard}
The curtains are made of thick, purple velvet.

The inside of this store is tasteful but austerely decorated, perhaps to better draw the eye towards the glass display case in the center of the room and the king's ransom in jewelry contained therein. You can leave to the west. {pieter-at-his-post}{pieter-bodyguard}
Light glitters across diamond-encrusted rings, bracelets, pendants, brooches, and necklaces spread out on black velvet.

Any one piece is several times more valuable than everything you've ever nicked in your entire life put together. The thought of wearing something that extravagant on your wrist makes your skin tingle.

The inside of this shop is dark — dark wood paneling on the walls; deep, wine-dark carpeting on the floor; even a pair of huge, leather armchairs over in one corner. The back half of the room is hidden behind a wall of reinforced wood, with a wide window cut through the center. {pieter-bodyguard}
The armchairs are overstuffed, upholstered in rich, dark leather.
(TODO during play-testing — A wine-dark carpet, thick enough to swallow a footstep, which is presumably the point.)

The window forms a sort of counter, with an ornately scrolled, brass grating that opens to the inside, allowing customers to speak with the proprietors on the other side. In fact, it appears that the only way to get service here is by standing up at the counter, so it's not exactly clear what the fancy chairs are for.
The carpet is deep, plush, and colored a rich, vibrant... pink.
Armless, headless torsos carved from wood, stuck atop iron tripods, and dressed in fancy clothes. They're actually a bit ghoulish, now that you really look at them.
In the clothier's tall, floor-length mirror, you can see yourself from head to toe.
The clothes here are lovely — rich velvets and flowing silks, dyed with brilliant colors and embroidered with lace and gems.

Tall, thin, and impeccably dressed, although his fashion sense seems a bit...decorative, compared to the more austere look preferred by men of Toresal's upper class. His hairline is receding, and what hair he has left is plastered back onto his scalp with fragrant oil. He looks as though he'd secretly prefer to wipe things down with a scented handkerchief before touching them; somehow, through good breeding and intestinal fortitude, he manages to soldier on despite not doing so.

Though in her elder years, Dame Sandler is still a tall and striking woman. Her long, silver hair is pulled back in a complicated bun, and she has a habit of inspecting her merchandise through a monocle on the end of a long, slender, gold-filigreed handle. Sometimes you wonder what she's doing running a shop (even such a relatively high-class one as this); her demeanor is more that of an aristocrat, if not full royalty.
Dame Sandler stands near the central display case. A small, dignified smile plays on her lips.

Pieter is loyal to Dame Sandler and tirelessly vigilant. You've traded friendly words with him in the past, but most of the time he stays quiet to preserve a sense of professionalism. He gives you a slight smile and nod when you catch his eye.

It's in some ways fortunate that you're not on a first-name basis with these fellows, because you'd never be able to tell them apart. Their faces are utterly identical, from the tops of their bald, cadaverous heads down to the black, dusty collars of their coats.
The Chorus Brothers hover behind their window, staring at you.
The city of Toresal.

A little-known shortcut between Lord's Market and the less affluent neighborhoods of the city's south end. A narrow street to the southwest leads to Maiden House, or you can return to the market square to the north. {bobby-leans}

Bobby is a few years older than you, a tall, broad-shouldered lad with tousled black hair and a rakish grin. He's an orphan, like you, and like you he makes the streets of the city his home and lives by his wits. Unlike you, he doesn't have the safety net of Maiden House to fall back on, but somehow he always seems to do well for himself.

You also happen to think that he's devastatingly handsome, although you would never admit that under the worst torture the King's interrogators could devise. He doesn't even know that you're really a girl, and you're not about to tell him, because if he knew he would certainly stop inviting you along on his exploits.
The alley dead-ends in a small courtyard surrounded by old, run-down buildings. You can return to the main part of the city to the northeast.
The buildings in this part of town have seen better days.

There's nothing on the outside to distinguish Maiden House from any of the other run-down tenements in this neighborhood, but you recognize it well. You grew up in this place, and it is filled with memories both good and bad. Well, okay, mostly bad. But you make do with what you have.
A battered wooden door provides entrance into the southern building. There's no sign, but you know it well nonetheless — this is the door to Maiden House, your 'home'.

The main hallway runs through the center of Maiden House, with several doorways leading to rooms on either side. To the southeast and southwest are the laundry and privy, respectively; to the northeast lies the kitchen; and to the northwest is the dormitory where you and the other orphans sleep.
The front door is closed and locked — and it will stay locked until sunup. The Widows give you a good bit of latitude generally, but curfew is one of the few rules they never, ever bend.

Widow Theresa is a harsh, sour-faced woman, with suspicious eyes and a mannish, angular jaw that she thrusts out when she is angry, which is nearly always. You gather that she was very poor before coming to Maiden House, and she harbors a bitter dislike for anyone whom she perceives as unjustly privileged. For reasons that persistently escape you, that includes you. Staying out of her way is generally the best tactic.
Widow Theresa stalks the hallway, her eye out for trouble.
That's the key to the front door. Widow Theresa keeps it on a ribbon around her neck constantly.
It's just a long piece of ribbon.
A long room lined with rough bunks, where the children sleep and, if they are too young to run about the city on their own, play. The main hallway lies southeast.
The bunks are spare and functional, straw mattresses on wooden frames. It's clean straw, but that's about all that can be said for them.
The bunks are spare and functional, straw mattresses on wooden frames. It's clean straw, but that's about all that can be said for them.

The kids are mostly younger than you. Some of them you saw earlier with Bobby. They sit up in their beds, whispering secrets to each other, showing off the childish treasures they found during the day: pebbles, pennies, bits of string. It almost makes you wish you could be that young again. Your life was so much less complicated then.
The other children are all sound asleep in their bunks.

A low-ceilinged room with a fire pit at one end for cooking, a basin at the other end for washing, and rows upon rows of pots and pans hanging from the rafters. The long table at the side of the room is where the children take their meals. You can leave to the southwest. {fiona-at-the-basin}

scenery in the Kitchen

The table seats about twenty hungry orphans, with room at the end for two or three scowling widows to enforce discipline. You rarely eat here, yourself. Older kids are encouraged to scrounge around the city for their meals rather than rely on the kitchen, but the Widows make sure that no one goes hungry.
Dozens of them, and you are familiar with each and every one. Scullery duty is not exactly your favorite day of the week.
The logs are down to glowing embers now.
The rafters are made of dark, rough wood.
The basin is filled with grayish, greasy water. It's not clear whether it's making the dishes more or less dirty.
The kids did a number on them tonight. Fiona is about halfway through the stack.

Fiona is a plump and genial woman, always quick with a smile or a bit of advice. The strange thing is, her advice always seems to make good sense, though sometimes you are loathe to admit it. She likes you and occasionally does you a good turn when you're in trouble with Widow Theresa.
Not much more than a narrow closet, with a hole in the floor and a bench over it. At least it's more private than an alley.

scenery in the Privy

The less said about that, the better.
The bench allows you to use the privy without a lot of ungainly squatting.

The window has been stuck halfway open for as long as you can remember. No one's ever bothered to fix it, because no matter how cold it gets, no one who's been in that privy would ever consider closing the window for even an instant. There's a bit less than two hand-widths of clearance between the pane and the sill — just enough for you to scrape through.
The air in here is filled with steam and the sharp stink of lye soap. Moisture trickles down the walls, and puddles of water splash underfoot. The main hallway lies northwest. {shannon-at-the-tub}
The wooden tub is huge enough to bathe in (and it has been used for that purpose on occasion). It's slopping over with soap-clouded water, pouring steam into the humid air.
The water is gray and coated with greasy-looking suds.
The clothes look as gray as the water they're floating in. It's hard to see how they ever actually get clean.
The constant steam makes everything in this room damp.
Dripping clothes hang from a simple clothesline stretched across the room.
The hanging clothes still look grungy, but at least they smell a bit nicer.

Shannon is the youngest of the widows in Maiden House. She is plain-looking, none too bright, and, to all appearances, utterly uninterested in ever remarrying, which is perhaps just as well. She devotes herself to the children, particularly the toddlers, and does most of the cleaning and cooking for Maiden House.
This tiny spur of an alleyway runs between the back of Maiden House and the high stone wall surrounding the park. You can make your way around to the Maiden House Entrance to the northeast.
The stone wall is about ten feet high.
The privy window is at ground level on the outside. Through the dirty glass, you can look down into the hole in the bathroom floor. Not that you'd want to.

At night, the normally crowded marketplace is an empty maze of shadows, abandoned stalls and rolled-up canvas. The Lord's Road lies north, and Commerce Street lies back east. {bobby-under-post} {pieter-bodyguard}
It's a little bit eerie, seeing the whole market empty and packed away like this.
It's huge, almost too big to put your arms around. Way up at the top, you can see wires stretching out in each of the cardinal directions.

The wide and well-paved Lord's Road runs from Grubber's Market straight north to Lord's Keep, a mile or so from the city. To the east are rolling pastures; to the west, broken ground and scrub. {bobby-waiting} {pieter-bodyguard}
The land to the west of Lord's Road is rocky and dry, no good for growing much of anything other than thornbushes.
The outer walls of Toresal are built of heavy, white stone.

This wide, open field is used by the city for tourneys and other holiday events, or by cattle-sellers driving their livestock to market. Tonight it is empty except for the occasional cow pie. To the north you can see the dark, rough edge of a forest. {bobby-waiting} {pieter-bodyguard}
Last time you checked, cow pies pretty much all looked the same.

A small stream bubbles out of the woods and cuts through the pasture's north end. The edge of the forest lies to the north, just across the water. The city is far away to the south. {bobby-waiting} {pieter-bodyguard}
The water is clean and clear, rippling over a shallow bed of stones and splashing over the larger rocks. It's only about ten feet wide here; you could probably pick your way across.
The stones just barely poke over the surface of the water, rounded and slippery.
You can just make out the silhouette of the city walls, far to the south.

You are in the woodlands just southeast of Lord's Keep, following the game trails that wind their way through strands of pale birch and black spruce. There is just enough moonlight trickling through the upper branches to see your way by. {sapling-north}{sapling-east}{sapling-west} {pieter-bodyguard}
The sapling is split down half its length, forming a distinctive 'Y' shape.
It's right next to a path leading north.
It's right next to a path leading east.
It's right next to a path leading west.
The trees grow thick and close all around you.
The trails are little more than narrow gaps in the underbrush, leading in every which direction.
One trail leads north, past a split sapling.
One trail leads east, past a split sapling.
One trail leads west, past a split sapling.
The underbrush is thick and tangled.

The woods open out here in a small, moonlit clearing. The ruins of an old pavilion lie here, pale pavestones poking up like bones from the grass. {fountain-closed}{fountain-open} {bobby-waiting} {pieter-bodyguard}

The fountain is shaped like a large bowl, topped with a classical-style statue of Brigid pouring water from an urn. Of course, the fountain is dry now, its stone cracked, the bowl filled with bird droppings and dead leaves. But at one time it must have been very beautiful.
One side of the stone plinth supporting the statue has opened up, revealing a narrow opening into darkness.
Whatever once stood here was probably very beautiful. Now it's just rubble in the grass.

The statue's features are worn away and obscured by moss, but you've seen enough statues of Brigid to know that she's almost always depicted carrying water. She cradles her urn like a child, tipping it gently over the bowl of the fountain.
One side of the stone plinth supporting the statue is open, revealing a narrow tunnel leading down into darkness.

The urn is hollow, and probably had water flowing out of it when the fountain worked.

Looking closely, you notice a small metal bolt sticking out of the bottom of the urn.
Just a little knob of metal, sticking out of the bottom of the urn.
The tunnel leads down into darkness.

The walls and floor are old, damp, and spotted with some sort of whitish fungus, and the air has a wet, sour smell to it. Steps lead up to the fountain above you. To the north, a long, low-ceilinged tunnel leads into the gloom. {bobby-waiting} {pieter-bodyguard}
The fungus grows in little clusters all over the damp walls.
The stairs lead back up to the clearing above.
The torch's flame throws weird, shivering shadows across the walls.
{tunnel-end-sealed}{tunnel-end-open} {bobby-waiting} {pieter-bodyguard}
It's a small metal bracket for holding a torch, bolted into the wall of the tunnel.
{wall-description-sealed}{wall-description-open}

The chapel of the Goddesses is a spacious, octagonal room, empty of furniture. The wood-paneled walls glow warmly, reflecting the light from dozens of devotional candles; the high ceiling disappears in the shadows overhead. A corridor leads southwest, and a secret passage in the south wall leads into subterranean gloom. {bobby-waiting} {pieter-bodyguard}
Little shelves built into the otherwise bare walls hold a number of devotional candles.

The candles sit on little shelves built into the otherwise bare walls. It is traditional to light a candle when offering a prayer to one of the Goddesses; each of these wavering points of light is someone's hope, a wish, a dream.
{bailey-in-shadow}{bailey-for-the-ball} {steps-stand} {steps-dash} {bobby-waiting} {pieter-bodyguard}
Steep stone steps climb up to the top of the wall.
The Lord's Guards are dressed in polished mail and tabards emblazoned with the Toresal coat of arms, and each one wears a hefty sword at his hip. Fortunately, they haven't noticed you. Yet.
You can't get near enough to do that without attracting the attention of the guards.

At the top of the wall you can lean out over the parapets and take in all the lands surrounding Toresal. It's a nice view, but torches set every few yards along the wall make this a dangerous spot to linger in. Stairs lead down into the courtyard below, and a dark archway opens to the north. {bobby-waiting}
Steep stone steps climb up to the top of the wall.
If you get anywhere near those torches, you'll be spotted in no time. Best to stay low and in the shadows.
It's an impressive view, no doubt, but you really don't have time to admire it right now.

The city is a pile of shadows in the distance, lit here and there with pinpricks of light: a guardsman carrying a torch, perhaps, or some night-owl sitting by the window with a lantern. Seeing it makes you realize just how absurd is your current predicament: you would be safe back in the city, snug in your bunk in Maiden House, or even skulking around the alleyways you know so well. Instead, you're breaking into Lord's Keep, sneaking along its walls, one slip-up away from getting yourself arrested or worse.
It's an impressive view, no doubt, but you really don't have time to admire it right now.
A narrow antechamber, with an open archway to the south and an iron-reinforced door to the north. Arrow slits to either side lend the door an important and dangerous air. {bobby-waiting}
The door is big and tough-looking, with bands of riveted iron across its thick wooden planks.

The arrow slits are rectangular holes in the wall, about two inches high and six inches wide. Someone on the inside could stick the end of a crossbow in there and fire at anyone out here, all the while being totally protected by the wall. Fortunately, no one is manning the slits right now.

From here, you can see flickering firelight through the arrow slit, and hear voices on the other side.

You can hear several voices coming from the room on the other side of the arrow slit — guards relaxing on break, probably.

'...and I says, I don't care who hired you, people are tryin' to do honest business here, and you're steppin' on toes. Take yer men and hit the road, or else you can continue searchin' for yer urchin boy in the city jail. And this tough fellow, him so hard with his sword and his scars and all, he just starts to cry, blubberin' like a frightened scullery maid!'

'Haw! Yer lyin', so you are!'

'Goddesses witness it, 'tis the truth! I could hardly credit it meself, and I weren't that impressed with the man to begin with. Go on, I says, and gave him a boot to the fundament to send him on his way.'

There is general laughter. You glance at Bobby, but he motions you to keep listening.

'You seen tomorrow's detail yet?'

'Yeah, dress-up duty. Polishing helmets so we can look all pretty for the lords and ladies coming down to Baron Fussypants' ball.'

'Not just lords and ladies, I heard. Word has it the Queen herself is on the guest list.'

'Oh, pull the other one.'

'Goddesses witness it. They say she's comin' down with her daughter in tow, that's why Fossville's hostin' the ball in the first place. He's tryin' to get in the Queen's good graces, so's he can marry the girl.'

'What, the Queen?'

'No, you dim. He wants to marry the Princess. Our Lord Fussypants is trying to position himself for the throne.'

'Well, he's welcome to it, long as I'm paid at week's end. Of course, I'm not looking forward to spending a night standing at attention for a horde of fancy, feathered fops to goggle and gaggle at, but I guess it's better than latrine duty...'

Bobby pulls you away. He's grinning, his eyes wide and his eyebrows cocked. Isn't it great?

But you're too nervous to care. There are who knows how many men of the Lord's Guard right on the other side of that door. Someone could walk out at any second. You grab Bobby's arm and give it a firm yank — It's time to go.
The guards' conversation has moved on to other things, and Bobby is motioning that you should leave.
A dank, cramped, foul-smelling cell. A pair of ragged burlap blankets and a few lumps of filthy straw litter the floor. The door is to the north. {jacobs-squats}{jacobs-stands}{jacobs-sulks}

Slowly the world comes back to you. You feel something cold and hard against your cheek; something gritty and scratchy under your hand. You hear footsteps on stone, muttering voices that fade in and out. Someone laughs, a raw, cruel sound. A loud squeak, and an echoing, metallic crash. The footsteps fade away.

You open your eyes. It's still dark.

No, it's just dim. Dim light trickles in from somewhere above you.

You sit up, and a tender spot on the back of your head throbs. Red and purple splotches bloom in front of your eyes, then fade away. After a moment or two, your head clears, and you can see where you are.

A dank, cramped, foul-smelling cell. A pair of ragged burlap blankets and a few lumps of filthy straw litter the floor. The door is to the north. {jacobs-squats}
The blankets are threadbare, filled with holes, and stained with Goddesses-know-what. You can hardly believe that anyone would actually cover themselves with something like this.
From the smell and the look of it, this straw is all prisoners ever get in the way of a toilet.
You can't see the thing that Jacobs threw from here: you'll have to poke around in the nasty stuff to find it.
It's a short bit of stiff wire, like the ones you've sometimes seen Bobby carrying around.
The south cell door is made of stout wood reinforced with bands of iron. A tiny viewing window in the upper half of the door allows guards to look in and prisoners to look out.
The north cell door is made of stout wood reinforced with bands of iron. A tiny viewing window in the upper half of the door allows guards to look in and prisoners to look out.
The west cell door is made of stout wood reinforced with bands of iron. A tiny viewing window in the upper half of the door allows guards to look in and prisoners to look out.

The jailhouse is hardly more comfortable than the cells themselves, just a crude, small room of unfinished stone, with a wooden bench and table for the guards. Cells are south, west, and north. A foul smell comes from a tiny alcove to the southwest, and a passageway to the east leads out. {jacobs-stands-here}
The furniture is rough and crudely carved.
The furniture is rough and crudely carved.
The east passage leads out to other areas of the prison... and hopefully to a way out.

A dank, cramped, foul-smelling cell. A pair of ragged burlap blankets and a few lumps of filthy straw litter the floor. The door is to the east.

Jacobs is a huge brute, with a face that looks young, but already grizzled and rough beyond his years. His wide, watery eyes jitter constantly. His lip is curled in a constant half-sneer, as though his confinement in jail is merely a passing diversion for him. His clothes, though stained and rumpled, seem too rich to belong to a common thug.

A short, bald-headed man, with a week's worth of stubble on his neck and a nose bright red from burst blood vessels. His breath reeks of cheap spirits, and his watery eyes shift constantly, as though always looking for a way out of his current predicament.

He's a tall, wobbly scarecrow of a man, with a huge nose, ears like jug handles jutting from the sides of his head, and a throat-apple the size of a child's fist that bobs up and down constantly. He never speaks; just smiles and nods whenever anyone says or does anything. You suspect he may be a few coins short of a full purse.
This tiny alcove reeks worse than the privy back at Maiden House, and that's saying something. The main room is back to the northeast. {grate-set}{grate-moved} {hole-uncovered}

The stonework around the metal grate is loose and crumbling.
You might be able to pull the grate free, if you really strained.
The hole is too dark and too deep for you to see the bottom, although you think you can hear the sound of running water coming from far below.
The colour Olmer named.
The glyphs, as they stand.

The tunnels down here are made of ancient, unmortared brick, slimy with centuries of filth and mold. Dim light trickles down through narrow vents in the ceiling. Side tunnels split off in numerous directions, twisting away into darkness.

Well, it can't be that much worse than rotting in prison, you think. You sit down and dangle your feet over the edge of the hole. You can hear the sound of running water, and smell the sharp stink of sewage. You offer a quick prayer to Brigid — Please give me a chance to clean up before seeing Bobby again — take a deep breath, and drop down into darkness.

The water is sluggish and cold, knee-deep in most places. Things float past you in the ooze — garbage, dead rats, and worse. You try to avoid the worst of it, but it's already soaked through your shoes. You feel like you'll never be clean of it.
The tunnel walls are slimy with filth and mold.

The symbols are a number of crude shapes, no bigger than your hand. Each one is painted on the wall next to one of the side tunnels, as if to mark the way.

'She... she got away from me, Miss Fiona,' wails Shannon. 'I was trying to get her into the hiding place, just like you said, but she slipped past me and wriggled out the privy window. You know how fast she can get through that window, Miss Fiona. She could be anywhere in the city by now. I'm so sorry, Miss Fiona, so sorry.'

You can't help but grin. You've always thought of Shannon as being a trifle dim-witted, and now you'll have to revise your opinion.

The mercenary captain utters a curse so foul that you actually wince. 'Don't just stand there, you bleeding dims,' he yells, 'get out there and find her! You two, keep an eye on the alley in case she comes back. Go! Go! Find her or I'll have your hides!' The footsteps run back up the hall, growing fainter this time, then vanishing altogether as they cross the threshold and exit Maiden House.

You let out a long, shaky breath.
